newsitem.title: UK: BA urges strike talks, sees delays Saturday.
newsitem.headline: BA urges strike talks, sees delays Saturday.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Thursday it was urging its main cabin crew union to renew negotiations over pay and a plan to save 42 million pounds ($71 million).
BA said it expected to see an improvement in services operating on Friday as it braced for the last day of a 72-hour cabin crew strike, but anticipated delays on Saturday.
BA officials told a news conference it had operated 25 percent more services on Thursday than Wednesday and confirmed it expected to run another 20 percent more on Friday.

Mike Street, BA director of operations, urged the British Airways Stewards and Stewardesses Association (BASSA) to hold talks with management over a new pay structure deal which a breakaway cabin crew union, Cabin Crew 89, has already accepted.

"We have an opportunity now to sort out the strike with BASSA. We have to have a better relationship...we're ready at any time to sit down and talk, but we won't unpick a deal we've discussed over five months," Street said.
The airline said it had chartered aircraft and was offering non-striking cabin crew taxis and hotel accommodation in order to ensure they turned up for work on Friday.
"We have more crew coming to work all the time," Street said.
He said 1,600 staff had come into work on Thursday while 250 had gone on strike. A further 1,700 had called in sick rather than report for work.
BA conceded that as a result of the strike, on Saturday only 75 percent of all its longhaul flights were likely to operate and 50 percent of shorthaul.
Street estimated the strike had already cost the carrier "considerably more than the pilots' dispute last year which didn't even become a strike".
The pilots' dispute is estimated to have cost BA 15 million pounds. Street could not give a precise estimate of the cost of the present strike, saying it was too soon to calculate.
He did, however, admit that the airline was likely to have lost goodwill with customers. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
"If there is an industrial dispute, flights don't fly and clearly customers are upset by it. But passengers are glad we gave them a fighting chance of avoiding disruption," Street said.
BA said it was still considering taking legal action over the legality of the strike ballot of cabin crew held by the Transport and General Workers Union.
"We are in touch with our lawyers and we've told the union we reserve our legal right to take action," Mervyn Walker, BA director of human resources, said.
The T & G senior representative George Ryde said earlier he was confident the strike ballot was legal and the union would win any legal action if a challenge was mounted by BA.
BA's Street said far fewer passengers had been stranded than the 25,000 on Wednesday because they had been given more notice and more services had been provided.
Meanwhile, BA said it expected the result of a ballot being held by ground staff over the sale of the airline's catering division at Heathrow would be announced later on Thursday.
